lesson.title: Numbers & Ages: 1–100
lesson.subtitle: Counting, prices, and expressing age as possession: tengo treinta años

hook.title: Why You 'Have' Your Years in Spanish
hook.content: In English, your age is something you ARE: 'I am thirty years old'. In Spanish (just like French and Italian), your years are treasures you HAVE accumulated and hold in your hands with tener: Tengo treinta años (word for word: 'I have thirty years'). Asking someone's age is ¿Cuántos años tienes? ('How many years do you have?')!

pattern.title: Diphthong Twins Inside the Numbers: Siete (7), Nueve (9), Diez (10), Cien (100)
pattern.content: Remember our stress-splitting vowel rule from Topic 10 (e → ie, o → ue)? Look at how it explains the numbers! Latin septem → siete (7), Latin novem → nueve (9, just like nuevo 'new'!), Latin decem → diez (10, English decimal), and Latin centum → cien (100, English century)!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin double -nn- in annus palatalized to /ɲ/ in Spanish, written ñ (originally a scribal shorthand of a small n written above the first n).
pattern.trap_note: Never omit the tilde on el año ('the year', /ˈaɲo/) — without the tilde on ñ, the word changes meaning completely!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: uno, cinco, siete, nueve, veinte / treinta, cien
exercises.meaning: one (un / una before a noun), five (quintet), seven (septem → e→ie), nine (novem → o→ue), twenty / thirty, one hundred (cent)
exercises.explanation: siete, nueve, diez, and cien all show the familiar e→ie and o→ue diphthong shifts.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I am twenty years old' in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: Age is possessed with tener: Tengo veinte años ('I have twenty years').

exercises.idea: ask a friend how old they are: 'How many years do you have?'
cues: How many (masculine plural to match años) → ¿Cuántos
exercises.explanation: ¿Cuántos años tienes? — cuántos agrees in masculine plural with años.

diagnosis.slip: used eres or estás for age
diagnosis.cue: Spanish never uses ser or estar for age — always use tener + años!

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Tengo treinta años'?
exercises.meaning: I am thirty years old (literal Spanish blueprint: I-have thirty years)
exercises.explanation: Spanish views age as the count of years you hold: Tengo treinta años.

summary.outcome: Count from 1 to 100 and ask and state ages using tener + años.

use_example.english: How old are you? — I am thirty years old.

summary.takeaway: In Spanish you are not 'years old' — you HAVE years (Tengo X años).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1501] Numbers 1 to 30): master counting 1–30 and see why uno drops its -o before masculine nouns.

twist.explanation: Tiene diez años ('He/she has ten years').

foreshadow.line: Next in Topic 16: the days of the week (named after the planets!) and how Spanish says 'on Monday' without a preposition.

payoff.text: Having crossed the Sentence Gate after Topic 14, you now enter Phase 3 (Time, Past & Comparison).

uno.english_meaning: one (un before m. noun, una before f. noun)
uno.etymology_derivation: Drops -o before a masculine noun: un libro.

tres.etymology_derivation: Shared Indo-European root with English three.

nueve.etymology_derivation: Latin novem diphthongized o → ue (just like nuevo 'new'!).

treinta.etymology_derivation: Numbers 31–99 join with y ('and'): treinta y uno.

cien.etymology_derivation: Bare cien before a noun (cien años) or alone; ciento before 1–99 (ciento dos).

año.english_meaning: year (tener X años: to be X years old)
año.context_translation: I am thirty years old (lit. I have thirty years).
año.etymology_derivation: Latin double -nn- evolved into Spanish palatal ñ (written with a tilde, originally a tiny n drawn above the first n!).

tengo.etymology_derivation: Latin teneō developed an epenthetic velar g: tengo.
